opus-5.5.text:
I think architecture research right now is in a very interesting but also quite difficult position.

The biggest practical challenge is that the bar for proving something works has become extremely high. The Transformer has been optimized for years: the kernels, the parallelism strategies, the training recipes, the hyperparameters. So when you propose a new architecture, say a linear attention variant or a state space model, you're not competing against the Transformer as an idea. You're competing against an entire ecosystem tuned around it. Even if your idea is good in principle, it can look worse at first simply because nobody has spent the same engineering effort on it.

The second challenge is scale. Many architectural differences only show up, or flip, at larger scales. Something can look great at 100 million parameters and disappear at a few billion, or the other way around. Academic labs usually can't afford to run experiments at the scale where industry actually makes decisions. So there's a gap: academia can generate ideas, but validating them convincingly needs compute that mostly sits in industry.

Third, evaluation is tricky. Perplexity alone isn't enough. For efficient architectures like linear attention, the real questions are about in-context retrieval, long-context reasoning, and how the model behaves after post-training or under RL. Those are expensive and noisy to measure, so it's easy to fool yourself in either direction.

And there's hardware efficiency, which I care a lot about. An architecture that is theoretically linear in sequence length but can't use tensor cores well won't win in practice. Much of my own work, like on gated linear attention and DeltaNet, has really been about making these models hardware-friendly, with chunkwise parallel algorithms, so they can actually train at speeds comparable to optimized attention. I think a lot of good ideas in the past died not because they were wrong, but because they were slow.

That said, I'm actually fairly optimistic about the prospects. A few things have changed. First, there's real demand now. With reasoning models and agents, sequences are getting very long, and inference cost, especially the KV cache, has become a real bottleneck. So efficiency isn't just an academic nicety anymore. Second, we've seen hybrid architectures, mixing some full attention layers with linear attention or state space layers, get adopted in serious production models. That's a strong signal that the field is willing to move beyond the pure Transformer when the trade-off makes sense.

Third, the theory has matured. We now understand much better how these models relate to each other. Linear attention, state space models, and fast-weight or test-time-training views can be unified under a common framework, and things like the delta rule give a principled way to improve memory capacity. That makes the design space less of a random search and more of a structured exploration.

So my overall view is: pure architecture search for its own sake is hard to justify, but architecture work tied closely to hardware efficiency and to concrete needs like long context and cheaper inference has a very bright future. I don't think the Transformer is the end point. The question is more what the right hybrid looks like and which components earn their place.

r001.rationale: The response says an architecture can look good at 100 million parameters and then disappear at a few billion, directly describing small-scale success failing at larger scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest practical challenge is that architecture research is one of the most expensive forms of research to validate. You can have a beautiful idea, something that looks clean on paper, and at small scale it beats the Transformer baseline by a point or two. But nobody believes small-scale results anymore, and they're right not to. The real question is always: does it hold at 7B, at 70B, at trillions of tokens? And the honest answer is that most academic groups, including the one I came from, simply cannot afford to run that experiment. So you end up in this awkward position where you can propose and you can argue, but the final verdict is rendered by whoever has the compute.

The second challenge is more subtle, and I think people underestimate it. The Transformer isn't just an architecture; it's an entire ecosystem. The kernels are optimized, the training recipes are tuned, the hyperparameters have been swept thousands of times by thousands of people. When you compare a new linear attention variant against a Transformer, you're not comparing two ideas on equal footing. You're comparing a one-year-old idea with a well-tuned eight-year-old industrial system. A lot of the "new architectures don't work" conclusions are really "we didn't spend enough effort on the infrastructure" conclusions. That's actually why I spent so much time on things like flash-linear-attention. If you don't write the hardware-efficient kernels yourself, your idea will lose on wall-clock time before anyone even looks at the loss curve, and then the conversation is over.

Then there's the inference side, which is where I'm actually most optimistic. The Transformer's KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. For short contexts, nobody cares. But once you're talking about long context, agents running for hours, reasoning models generating tens of thousands of tokens, the memory cost becomes a real economic problem, not just an academic one. Linear attention, state space models, delta rule variants, these have constant memory per step. So for the first time, the motivation isn't "wouldn't it be elegant if attention were linear." The motivation is "our serving bill is enormous." That changes who's willing to listen.

As for prospects, I think the realistic future is not that something replaces attention wholesale. It's hybrids. You keep a small number of full-attention layers, because softmax attention is genuinely good at precise retrieval, at copying, at looking up a specific token from far back. And you use linear or recurrent layers for everything else, because most layers don't need that capability and shouldn't pay for it. We've already seen this direction in several production models, and I expect that to become the default rather than the exception.

What I find encouraging is that the theoretical understanding has caught up a lot in the last two years. We used to just try things. Now we understand, for example, why plain linear attention forgets, why a gating mechanism helps, why the delta rule gives you something closer to an associative memory that can actually overwrite old information rather than just accumulating it. When you understand the mechanism, you can design more deliberately instead of random searching. That's what makes me think architecture research is actually in a healthier state now than it was when everyone was just proposing another attention variant and hoping.

r001.rationale: The response says small-scale wins are not convincing and that large-scale validation is often unaffordable, but it does not state that algorithms that work at small scale often fail at large scale.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest practical challenge is that an architecture is difficult to evaluate in isolation. You’re also choosing a training recipe, a data mixture, and an implementation. If a new architecture performs worse, is the idea itself worse, or have you simply spent much less time tuning it? And if it performs better at a small scale, you still have to establish whether that advantage survives when you scale it up.

There’s also a gap between an elegant idea and something that runs efficiently. A design might reduce the theoretical amount of computation but introduce operations that are difficult to execute efficiently on the hardware. So you need fairly tight feedback between the modeling work and the systems work, which makes experimentation expensive.

But I’m optimistic about the prospects. The useful question is: what specific constraint are you trying to improve? Memory usage, inference cost, the ability to process longer sequences? If you choose a clear target, you can design experiments that tell you something meaningful without immediately training the largest possible model.

For me, the key is to keep room for exploration while being disciplined about the evidence. A promising small experiment is a reason to investigate further; showing a practical advantage requires a much more complete comparison.

r001.rationale: The response says a small-scale advantage must be checked at larger scale, but it does not communicate that algorithms that work at small scale often fail at large scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest practical challenge is getting a reliable signal from an experiment. It’s easy to propose a change to an architecture, but much harder to tell whether it actually helps. You have to tune it, train it long enough, and compare it with a strong baseline under a fair compute budget. Otherwise, you may just be measuring which configuration received more attention.

There’s also a gap between an idea that looks efficient mathematically and one that runs efficiently on hardware. An architecture might use fewer operations but still be slower because the implementation or memory access patterns are less favorable. So architecture research increasingly involves systems work as well.

That said, I’m optimistic. There are still useful questions to explore around memory, long sequences, and how models allocate computation. The practical approach is to start with a clear hypothesis, test it cheaply, and then check whether the benefit survives at larger scales. Small experiments can guide you, but you have to be careful about assuming their conclusions will carry over.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that small-experiment conclusions may not carry over to larger scales, but it does not say that algorithms that work at small scale often fail at large scale.
